raw_case_text:
A 78-year-old male patient was referred to the Imam Reza Hospital, North Khorasan University of Medical Sciences, Bojnurd, Iran, for evaluation of disseminated skin lesions over the arm and hemithorax. As shown in Figure 1 , he presented with one-month history of multiple skin lesions, which started with a small furuncle on the left forelimb which progressed to other parts of the arm and hemithorax. He was originally resident in Esfarayen city in the Northeastern region of Iran, which is one of the new endemic regions of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL). The patient declared that prior to the dissemination of the lesion, he had edema and lymphedema over the arm and hemithorax. Physical examination was remarkable for mild peripheral edema and lymphedema, but in radiological and laboratory tests, there were no abnormalities. At the time of physical examination, mild peripheral edema and lymphedema, but no systemic symptoms such as fever, hepatosplenomegaly were observed; however, he had a 10-year history of opium smoking abuse, as well as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD ) which had previously been treated with Salbutamol (100 microg/4 times (puffs) per day) and Fluticasone/Salmeterol Spray (250/50 microg twice a day). The patient was hospitalized with an initial suspicion of diffuse bacterial infection due to lymphedema, opium smoking and history of respiratory disease. Physical examination showed that he had multiple, disseminated and wet-looking skin lesions which were papular, crusted and severely ulcerated all over the left arm and hemithorax ( Figure 1 ). Furthermore, the patient's lesions spread to his palm and all over the left finger nails which are very rare manifestations. It should be noted that three days before referring to the hospital, the patient bandaged up the lesions with plastic covers; therefore, all covered parts turned into creamy, wet-looking and severely inflammatory lesions which looked like second-degree burn wounds.
A hypothesis of leishmaniasis was made, and further evaluation by direct examination of the skin of the wrist and forearm using lesion scraping by a vaccinostyle, under sterile conditions was performed (Giemsa staining) revealing abundant intracellular Leishmania amastigotes inside and outside host cells (3+ parasitemia grade: 1-10 parasites/microscopic field) ( Figure 2A ). In addition, for histopathological examination, punch biopsy of lesions of the wrist and forearm were performed (Hematoxylin and Eosin staining: H&E). Histopathological smears of wrist and forearm skin lesions revealed mild hyperkeratotic epidermis based on dermis infiltrated by numerous mixed inflammatory cells including abundant macrophages at dermis filled with amastigote forms of Leishmania ( Figure 2B ). Direct microscopy skin smears for acid-fast bacilli were negative. According to positive Giemsa-stained slide and skin biopsy, diagnosis of diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) was made Bone marrow aspiration showed no detectable Leishmania parasites among myelogenous elements. All routine laboratory tests of the patient were normal. Viral markers (HIVAb, HBSAg, HCVAb), and anti-Brucella Ab (Wright, Coombs Wright and 2-mercaptoethanol) were negative. In addition, serous fluid from the patient's skin lesion were cultured in Schneider's Drosophila medium (Sigma, Darmstadt, Germany), supplemented with 5% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (HI-FBS) (Sigma, Germany). Isolated parasites were subcultured and monitored regularly to check promastigotes growth. In this experiment, 2 x 10 parasites/mL at the logarithmic (2 days) growth phases were counted and used for DNA extraction.
Total genomic DNA of Leishmania parasites was extracted from cultured parasites and also from paraffin-embedded blocks of the patient's skin biopsy using the GF-1 DNA extraction kit (GF-1, Vivantis, Canada), and Leishmania ITS1 was amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). For identification of Leishmania species by PCR-RFLP, the PCR product was digested using HaeIII ( BsuRI ) enzyme   ; L. major parasites were identified as the causative agents of DCL.
The patient's first PCR product was subjected to sequence analysis using the forward and reverse primers according to the manufacturer's instructions (Bioneer, South Korea). GenBank was searched for similar sequences and a significant similarity was found with other Leishmania species. The patient's ITS1 sequence was similar to the Iranian strain of L. major (AB04/HU64) (99%).
The patient was initially treated with a bilayer wet dressing that was coated with silver sulfadiazine and petroleum salve/ointment along with vancomycin (1 g/kg/per 12 h) and ceftriaxone (1 g/kg/per 12 h) as broad spectrum antibiotics. At the same time, he received antileishmanial therapy including: meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime) 20 mg/kg/day for 10 days. Since he showed no significant improvement with Glucantime and developed pancytopenia as a complication of therapy, his treatment was discontinued at day 10. Consequently, he was placed on amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/per day for 10 days) and showed progressive and marked improvement of cutaneous lesions ( Figure 3 ).
During hospitalization and successful treatment, he developed a severe lung infection and disseminated bronchiectasis probably due to his history of opium abuse and COPD; therefore, he was admitted to ICU and unfortunately died because of a systemic bacterial superinfection.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 78-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of disseminated skin lesions over his left arm and hemithorax.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 78-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of multiple skin lesions originating as a furuncle on the left forearm and disseminating to the arm and hemithorax. Prior to dissemination, he noticed edema and lymphedema over the arm and hemithorax. Three days before admission, he bandaged the lesions with plastic wrapping, resulting in macerated, wet, inflammatory lesions resembling second-degree burns. He was hospitalized with initial suspicion of diffuse bacterial soft tissue infection.
subjective.past_medical_history: Resident of Esfarayen, North Khorasan, Iran (endemic for cutaneous leishmaniasis). 10-year history of opium smoking abuse. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) managed with inhaled salbutamol (100 mcg 4 puffs/day) and fluticasone/salmeterol (250/50 mcg BID). Pre-existing left upper extremity lymphedema.
subjective.review_of_systems: Disseminated ulcerated skin lesions, localized lymphedema. Denied fever, chills, night sweats, or visceral symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple, disseminated, wet-looking, creamy inflammatory lesions that were papular, crusted, and severely ulcerated across the left arm, hemithorax, left palm, and all left fingernails, resembling second-degree burns. Mild peripheral edema and localized lymphedema over the left arm and hemithorax. Afebrile; no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine hematological, biochemical, and radiological examinations were normal. Viral serologies negative for HIV, HBsAg, and HCV. Anti-Brucella antibodies (Wright, Coombs Wright, 2-mercaptoethanol) negative. Direct microscopy of skin smears for acid-fast bacilli was negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Direct skin scraping of wrist and forearm lesions (Giemsa staining) revealed abundant intracellular and extracellular microorganisms (3+ parasitemia: 1-10 parasites/field). Punch biopsy of wrist and forearm lesions (H&E) showed mild epidermal hyperkeratosis and dermal infiltration by mixed inflammatory cells with abundant macrophages filled with intracellular organisms. Bone marrow aspiration revealed no detectable parasites. Skin lesion fluid cultured in Schneider's Drosophila medium with 5% HI-FBS yielded 2 x 10^7 flagellated organisms/mL at log phase.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) with unusual palmar and ungual involvement caused by Leishmania major, complicated by secondary bacterial infection.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Giemsa-stained scrapings and H&E punch biopsies revealed abundant Leishmania amastigotes (3+ grade); culture in Schneider's medium confirmed promastigotes; ITS1 PCR-RFLP with HaeIII and DNA sequencing demonstrated 99% identity with Leishmania major (Iranian strain AB04/HU64). Bone marrow aspirate was negative for Leishmania.
Differentials Ruled Out: Severe diffuse bacterial burn/cellulitis, cutaneous tuberculosis/leprosy (negative AFB), brucellosis, viral hepatitis/HIV, and visceral leishmaniasis (negative bone marrow).
Treatment & Clinical Course: Initial treatment included broad-spectrum antibiotics (IV vancomycin 1 g/12h and ceftriaxone 1 g/12h) and silver sulfadiazine dressings. Meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime; 20 mg/kg/day) was started but discontinued at day 10 due to poor response and drug-induced pancytopenia. Switched to intravenous amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/day for 10 days), achieving progressive and marked resolution of skin lesions. However, during hospitalization, the patient developed severe pulmonary infection and disseminated bronchiectasis related to COPD and opium abuse, and died in the ICU from systemic bacterial superinfection.
